messages.author: 253141a6efac547e
messages.subject: Fitted and predicted values from observed variable SEMs
parts:
All,

I know there’s been some back and forth about fitted, predicted, and residual values from observed variables in lavaan. As part of my course, I’ve whipped up three methods:

fitted_lavaan
predict_lavaan
residuals_lavaan

I haven’t put them into the main codebase yet, as I thought I’d see if either a) folk found this useful or b) if people who have worked with the main codebase more than I wanted to insert it - say, using residuals(mod, “fit”) or something.

Looking at how lavPredict generates factor scores, I think it might be straightforward to extend this to models with latent variables, although the ordering part of the functions might need to be reworked.

Anyway, let me know what you all think, and, Yves, as always I hope you find this useful. I’ll see if I can work it in and fork/pull if so.

-Jarrett

Hi Jarrett,

Thanks a lot for this contribution. I was waiting for this for a year so I will use soon. The only problem that I have is that I am using latent variables with single observed variables and I should adapt your functions to that situation (I do not know if I will be able). Do you think it would be easy to adapt the code to that situation?
We have predicted endogenous variables in a recent work (under review) and we compared the prediction performance of SEM with single multiple linear regression models of the endogenous variables. In term of covariation (modelled variance-covariance matrix) SEM reproduces it much better than MLR, however, in term of predicted values the models are almost equal, since we did not consider the model residuals. We could only reproduce the covariation if we took a stochastic simulation approach and simulate possible realities of the endogenous variables.
Does this function take into account the model residuals? Would it be different the prediction of endogenous variables using SEM or MLR models?

Kind regards,

Marcos

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Fitted and predicted values from observed variable SEMs
parts:
On 12/03/2016 11:33 AM, Jarrett Byrnes wrote:
> I haven’t put them into the main codebase yet, as I thought I’d see if
> either a) folk found this useful or b) if people who have worked with
> the main codebase more than I wanted to insert it - say, using
> residuals(mod, “fit”) or something.

Thanks Jarrett for contributing the code. I am sure some folks will find
it useful. Just a few remarks:

- if you have z <- y <- x, there seems to be (at least) two ways when it
comes to creating predictions:

1) the first way only provides 'newdata' for the 'pure' exogenous
variable(s) (here: only x); x then predicts y, and these predicted
values of y in turn predict z (I think this is what your code does)

2) the second way provides 'newdata' for all 'predictor' variables (y
and x); the newdata for x predicts y (and this is shown in the output),
but the newdata of 'y' predicts z

3) any combination of 1) en 2) can make sense, depending on the setting

- your approach seems to assume a recursive model

- categorical endogenous variables (binary/ordinal) need special
treatment; depending on 1), 2) or 3) above, care is needed to maintain
the categorical nature of the variables

- latent variables obviously complicate matters; several methods can be
used to 'estimate' them (this is what lavPredict() currently does), and
we may have the z <- y <- x setting too at the latent level

- several approaches to deal with missing data are possible

A general solution, therefore, is much more complicated than often
thought. When I implement a `prediction' function (in the regression
sense) in lavaan, it will need to address all these above points.
Somewhere in 2017, I hope to find the time to study this 'prediction'
problem in more detail.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Fitted and predicted values from observed variable SEMs

Thanks for the reply. In my case I have latent variables only for endogenous variables in order to be able to include the measurement error of that variables. So, I have the measured soil organic carbon (OC.m) and the real value of soil organic carbon (OC.r). It affected by other endogenous variables, such as clay (Clay.r -> Clay.m), and for deterministic exogenous variables, such as terrain altitude, slope, distance to the river, etc. My goal is to predict OC.m and Clay.m in locations with unknown values of the endogenous variables. I am interested on the measured variables rather than the latent variables, since I can only validate measured variables at some locations with independent data (Is this assumption correct in your view?).
When you use lavPredict() you have to provide all the variables (if I understand correctly), also endogenous variables, for this reason I would be interested in case 1) mentioned by Yves.
I really appreciate your help and I do not pretend you to adapt the function for my specific case, but rather to show that a case where this functionality may be useful. I think that there may be a lot of interest to use lavaan for studying and predicting spatial processes.

Kind regards,
Marcos

All,

I know there’s been some back and forth about fitted, predicted, and residual values from observed variables in lavaan. As part of my course, I’ve whipped up three methods:

fitted_lavaan
predict_lavaan
residuals_lavaan

I haven’t put them into the main codebase yet, as I thought I’d see if either a) folk found this useful or b) if people who have worked with the main codebase more than I wanted to insert it - say, using residuals(mod, “fit”) or something.

Looking at how lavPredict generates factor scores, I think it might be straightforward to extend this to models with latent variables, although the ordering part of the functions might need to be reworked.

Anyway, let me know what you all think, and, Yves, as always I hope you find this useful. I’ll see if I can work it in and fork/pull if so.
